intro: Frost on a window, a train to heaven, a hymn interrupted by a circus: Hawthorne’s stories set Ives’s piano loose. This scherzo runs from delicate black-key clusters to ragtime played with fists.

sections.label: Intro · Arpeggios across a frosted window
sections.mNote: Rapid piano figures begin Hawthorne’s fantastic scenes

sections.label: A · Soft clusters above a melody
sections.mNote: Neighbouring black keys sound high above a slower tune

sections.label: B · A rag with displaced accents
sections.mNote: Fast syncopations pull against the piano’s beat

sections.label: C · A hymn interrupts the rag
D · March, ragtime, then fists
sections.mNote: A march leads towards the great cluster climax

sections.label: E · Columbia starts in fragments
sections.mNote: The left hand introduces scraps of the patriotic song

sections.label: F · Columbia grows easier to recognise
sections.mNote: Longer phrases emerge from the piano’s interruptions

sections.label: Coda · Triplets race across the keyboard
sections.mNote: Fragments of tunes fly through the final rush

cues.title: Frost on the window
cues.text: Arpeggios whirl across the piano. Ives links the opening to the children in Hawthorne’s The Three Golden Apples, waking to frost on the window. The glittering figures soon set a train-like motion running.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Hawthorne”: Ives’s identification of the opening arpeggios with the frosted window and the following railway music. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A board on black keys
cues.text: The score calls for a felt-covered board, fifteen inches long, to press neighbouring black keys high on the piano. The clusters sound softly while a slower melody moves below. A handful of clashing notes can make a remarkably gentle accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: first slow episode, fifteen-inch felt-covered board, high black-key clusters and lower melody. This describes the score’s technique; the recording credits do not specify Liang’s implement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano starts ragging
cues.text: The slow melody breaks into a fast rag. Accents arrive just before the beat, jostling the piano’s forward motion. Ives keeps changing the tunes while those displaced accents do their mischief.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: fast rag after the cluster episode and Ives’s use of ragtime syncopation. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Heaven by railway
cues.text: Hawthorne’s The Celestial Rail-Road, published in 1843, makes Bunyan’s arduous pilgrimage into a comfortable train ride. The passengers can stow their sins with the luggage. Ives’s scherzo borrows the train’s bustle and the story’s irreverence.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”, summarises the story, its publication date and its place in Ives’s scherzo. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: A hymn stops the dance
cues.text: The rag is interrupted by the quiet hymn Martyn, associated with the words “Jesus, lover of my soul”. Its shape resembles the sonata’s recurring melody. The busy piano music breaks back in, and the hymn interrupts again.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: two Martyn quotations interrupt the rag; the hymn’s opening words and resemblance to the human-faith melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A hymn against the circus
cues.text: In his 1920 Hawthorne essay, Ives pictures an old hymn haunting a churchyard while a circus parade comes down Main Street. The hymn shelters the people among the graves from the parade’s noise.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Hawthorne”, final paragraph: the churchyard hymn and circus parade. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#hawthorne

cues.title: A march, then more ragtime
cues.text: A march steps out of the ragtime, with piano clusters imitating drums. It slows to a pause before a longer rag begins. That passage works towards the great eruption of fist clusters.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the march, drum-like clusters, pause and renewed ragtime ending in the fist-cluster climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Columbia comes in pieces
cues.text: After the cluster climax, the piano starts slowly again. The left hand introduces phrases of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean. The patriotic tune begins to take shape among the fragments.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the slow restart after the fist clusters and Columbia phrases in the left hand. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The scraps become a song
cues.text: Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean grows more recognisable as its phrases accumulate. Ives works backwards from the usual theme and variations: the tune emerges after its pieces have already been tossed around the piano.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: progressive recognition of Columbia, discussed through J. Peter Burkholder’s term cumulative form. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tunes inside the whirlwind
cues.text: Rapid triplet figures race across the keyboard, carrying scraps of familiar tunes with them. Near the end, Columbia and the quiet hymn make their last appearances before a final splash across the piano.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”, final paragraph: complex triplet figures, Columbia references, hymn reminiscence and closing joke. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Black keys held above a tune
transitions.from: Intro · Arpeggios across a frosted window
transitions.to: A · Soft clusters above a melody
transitions.how: The rapid piano figures stop racing. In the slow episode, neighbouring black keys sound softly high on the keyboard, pressed together with a felt-covered board. A languid melody moves beneath the cluster, at a quite different pace from the opening arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: opening arpeggios and first slow cluster episode. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The piano breaks into a rag
transitions.from: A · Soft clusters above a melody
transitions.to: B · A rag with displaced accents
transitions.how: The soft high clusters and slow lower melody break into fast ragtime. Accented notes fall just before the beat, making the piano lurch forward. The held black-key chords are replaced by quick, sharply articulated phrases.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the fast rag follows the slow cluster passage; his discussion explains its displaced accents. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Martyn interrupts the rag
transitions.from: B · A rag with displaced accents
transitions.to: C · A hymn interrupts the rag
transitions.how: The piano’s ragtime breaks off for a quiet statement of Martyn. The hymn’s longer notes resemble the sonata’s recurring melody. The rag returns between two hymn statements, so each passage interrupts the other.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: two quiet Martyn quotations interrupt the rag. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: A march steps out of the rag
transitions.from: C · A hymn interrupts the rag
transitions.how: The rag’s third continuation leads abruptly into a march. Piano clusters imitate drum strokes beneath its firmer tread. The march slows to a pause, then a longer ragtime passage begins and works towards the fist-cluster climax.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the third rag continuation, march, pause and renewed ragtime. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Fists stop, a tune starts
transitions.how: The long ragtime passage culminates in fist clusters. Afterwards the piano begins slowly again, and the left hand introduces phrases of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean. The patriotic song arrives a little at a time.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: fist-cluster climax, slow restart and Columbia phrases in the left hand. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: The left hand pieces Columbia together
transitions.to: F · Columbia grows easier to recognise
transitions.how: The piano develops the left hand’s scraps of Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean into increasingly recognisable phrases. The song grows clearer as the music gathers speed and force around it, with interruptions still breaking up its course.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”: the late cumulative treatment of Columbia. The existing section boundary divides this extended passage. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Triplets sweep across the piano
transitions.from: F · Columbia grows easier to recognise
transitions.to: Coda · Triplets race across the keyboard
transitions.how: After the play with Columbia, complex triplet figures take over the piano. Fragments of tunes pass through the running notes. The long rush continues towards the last recalls of the patriotic song and hymn.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Hawthorne”, closing paragraph: the triplet whirlwind and final tune references. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

sources.locator: Hawthorne section: opening, quiet clusters, ragtime, Martyn interruptions, march, fist-cluster climax, cumulative Columbia material and closing rapid figuration. Literary interpretations are distinguished from Ives’s own statements. Chronology distinguishes composition and editions.

sources.title: Charles Ives — Essays Before a Sonata
sources.locator: Introduction calls Hawthorne a scherzo; the Hawthorne essay’s final paragraphs distinguish the novelist’s moral subject matter from the fantastic realm attempted by this movement. The modern prefatory biographical sketch is not used as Ives’s testimony.

sources.title: Jan Swafford — Ives The Man: His Life
sources.locator: ‘like father, like son’: the remembered childhood story of playing drum parts with fists on the piano, explicitly reported as Ives’s own account.

composer.epithet: He sold life insurance in New York and wrote music in which a hymn across the river could outlast a whole marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut. Charles, born there in 1874, grew up with a father for whom a wrong note could be the beginning of an experiment.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, putting the tune of God Save the King through a teenager’s display of keyboard tricks. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and how to sustain a symphony. His First Symphony was the result: a young American speaking fluent European. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term. His son kept talking about him for the next sixty years.
